components.gap: Pearl treats this same chain (Fig. 2(a)) on p. 106, inside the cited extent secs. 3.1-3.2.3, pp. 103-112, with a d-separation illustration on its diagram with disturbances that the route does not supply: the path U_Z->Z->X->Y is blocked by S={Z} and by S={X}, so the corresponding independencies of a disturbance from Y (printed 'U_X indep Y | Z', apparently a misprint for U_Z, and 'U_Z indep Y | X') hold in every distribution the model can generate, however the arrows are parametrized; the path U_Z->Z->X<-U_X is blocked by the empty set but not by {Y}, so U_Z indep U_X holds while U_Z indep U_X | Y may fail; and this collider handling is named Berkson's paradox (Berkson 1946) and illustrated by two independent coins made dependent by the testimony that at least one is a tail. On the route the chain material (finite-causal-models.tex 812-950) derives only Z indep Y | X (thm:p15-w02c-p15-009-chain-testable item 1, d-separation remark at 917-922); the causal diagram with disturbance vertices (181-212) is never used for a d-separation statement; and the collider example thm:p16-collider-numerical-example (graphical-separation-adjustment.tex 264-298) neither names Berkson's paradox nor cites Berkson (1946). The entry itself (812-853) and its other source variants (eqs. (5)-(7), (11)-(13), (16)-(17), the seven-assumption testability claim, the p. 111 conclusions) are fully supplied.
